Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: kickoff — Preliminary traffic shape and SLA questions

Thanks Sean — quick context from our side: our beta has two main call patterns: (1) user-chat (avg. 380 tokens/request, long-tail up to 2.5k), 60% of traffic; (2) embedding+rerank (request pairs of short inputs, ~40 tokens each), 25%; (3) async batch scoring for offline features, 15% (large payloads but not latency sensitive).

Our target SLOs for GA are p95 <= 300ms for chat generation and p99 <= 1.2s; embeddings can be p95 <= 150ms. We're evaluating a fixed monthly commit but need a recommended headroom and guidance on burst capacity — we saw a few microbursts in beta (2–4x baseline for ~30s).

Do you have a first-pass tokens/sec estimate and suggested committed slab that balances cost vs. SLA? Also, is prefix caching effective for our chat patterns?

— Lena
Product Operations, Granary Labs

From: Sean Gallagher <sean.gallagher@redwoodinference.com>
To: Lena Park <lena@granary.ai>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2027-08-05T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: kickoff — Preliminary traffic shape and SLA questions

Lena — thanks for the traffic breakdown, that's very helpful. High-level answers up front then an attached spreadsheet with modelled scenarios (see granary_compute_model.xlsx):

- Baseline tokens/sec (TPS equivalent): using your weighted mix and conservative per-request tokens we estimate baseline token throughput of ~45k tokens/sec. That maps to ~9k chat requests/sec (assuming 5 tokens/gen/sec nominal per request for generation; see assumptions tab).
- SLO fit: to hit p95<=300ms on your primary chat model (Llama-variant, 8-bit quantized), we'd recommend provisioning for sustained throughput of ~1.7x baseline to absorb normal variability and warm-up costs. For p99 protection and 30s microbursts, add a burst buffer (auto-burst) capable of 3–4x baseline for short windows.
- GPU mapping: with our conservative kernel/sequence sizing, a single A100-equivalent slab (our reference) supports ~8–10k tokens/sec for chat workloads at target latency when caching is cold. With KV prefix caching (effective for repeat prompts), effective tokens/sec per GPU can rise by ~30% for your traffic mix — so plan for cache-friendly gains but don't rely on them for commit sizing.

I attached a sheet with three scenarios: conservative (1.9x baseline), nominal (1.5x), and aggressive (1.25x) including quantization tradeoffs and prefix-cache uplift. Bottom line recommendation for a committed slab: nominal plan -> commit equivalent to 8 A100-e slabs + 2 on-call burst slabs (reserved but cold-startable), which gives ~1.5x baseline sustained plus short 3x burst cushion via autoscaling.

I'll walk through the assumptions in a follow-up note — copying our infra lead Kimberly to align on ops/rollback playbook.

Thanks,
Sean
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Quick notes after scanning the model:

- Tail latencies: your p99 target is aggressive given long-tail chat tokens. We model p99 = f(cold-cache, seq-length, concurrent KV lookups). For the 2.5k long-tail requests, we recommend isolating those on a different instance pool (low concurrency) to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Cold start vs warm pool: we recommend a small warm pool of 2 slabs per region to reduce cold-start p95 variance; autoscale-to-zero is okay for non-latency-critical workloads but risky for chat p95.
- Throttles & graceful degradation: build route-level throttles to fall back to a smaller model variant (lower tokens/sec cost) with deterministic quality delta — this reduces required committed slabs and lowers cost while preserving availability.

Ben — can you run the cost delta for nominal vs conservative commits with our current pricing assumptions and include committed discount scenarios? I'll add the rollout playbook to mutual_action_plan.docx and share a first draft.

— Kimberly
Head of Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Granary deal: GPU slate simulation & surge absorption

Following up with the cost breakdown (high level):

- Nominal (8 slabs committed): estimated monthly committed cost = $76,500 before discounts. Includes 1.5x sustained headroom.
- Conservative (12 slabs committed): $112,000 monthly; provides 2x sustained headroom and more comfortable p99 margins for non-cacheable long-tail.
- We modeled burst autoscaling using reclaimed spare capacity and short-term preemptible slabs (price-effective) for 3–5 minute bursts — that reduces committed cost by ~12% vs buying pure reserved burst capacity.

Operational consideration: if Granary requires p99 <= 800ms instead of 1.2s, cost steps up ~22% at nominal commit due to higher required per-GPU allocation and warm pool sizing.

Next steps: propose Nominal commit with a 3-month ramp: start with 8 committed slabs + 2 on-call warm slabs, monitor token velocity and tail latency during ramp, then decide month 2 whether to move to 10 slabs.

— Ben
Principal Commercial Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks team — that level of detail helps a lot. A couple of quick clarifications before we lock the MAP:

1) Can you include a short scenario that shows costs if we rely on prefix caching heavily (50% effective) vs minimal caching? We want to understand downside if early production cache hit rates are lower.
2) For the long-tail 2.5k token requests, separating into a low-concurrency pool makes sense — how much incremental cost does that add for p95/p99 protection?

If the nominal path keeps cost within our budget with those caveats we can sign the initial 3-month commit. We'll aim to provide a sample production trace (1 day) next week to refine numbers.

— Lena
Product Operations, Granary Labs
